newsitem.title: USA: White House presses for trade authority by year-end.
newsitem.headline: White House presses for trade authority by year-end.

text.p: The White House is preparing an all-out campaign to calm political jitters about free trade and win congressional approval of new trade negotiation authority by the end of the year.

Jason Berman, the Recording Industry Association of America executive tapped by the White House to run the campaign for the so-called fast-track trade negotiation legislation, said the goal is to get it enacted by mid-November.

But first the administration has to submit proposed legislation to Congress. Berman said the plan is to do that during the week of Sept. 8, when lawmakers will have returned from a monthlong summer recess. President Bill Clinton plans to kick off the drive with a major trade speech.

When Congress gives fast-track authority to a president, it gives up the right to amend trade agreements and can only vote for or against them. The Clinton administration has been without fast-track authority since 1994.
The administration has said it needs fast-track authority to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) to include Chile as well as other trade deals.

But criticism of NAFTA by labor unions, consumer advocacy groups and some conservative Republicans as well as reports of plant closings and job losses in the United States have made many lawmakers wary of voting for fast-track authority.
Administration officials hopes to counter their nervousness by promoting the economic benefits of trade and the need for the negotiating authority to open overseas markets to U.S. exports.
They will also point to moves by the European Union and Japan to solidify their own trade ties around the world and with Latin America in particular.
A booming economy and the lowest unemployment rate in close to 25 years will likely help the administration's argument.

"There is an irony that at a time when we are at our most competitive and should be our most aggressive at breaking down barriers, there seems to be some hesitation on the part of lawmakers, but I believe that hesitation will be overcome," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in an interview.

In addition to the NAFTA expansion, the administration is seeking fast-track authority for a whole range of trade negotiations, including an upcoming global round of talks on farm trade and the completion of a pact to create a free-trade group combining North and South America.

A big sticking point has been how to deal with labor and environmental issues. Republicans want to limit authority to deal with those issues in trade negotiations, while Democrats want broad negotiating authority.
For the White House, the trick is to develop language for the legislation that will satisfy Republican concerns without driving a wedge between the Democrats.

The two leading Democrats in the House, Minority Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri and Minority Whip David Bonior of Michigan, oppose fast-track authority that does not specifically include labor and environmental issues.
Cabinet members are expected to fan out across the country starting in September in an effort to build public support. Officials said Clinton will also be actively working on the issue.

But even during August while lawmakers are on recess, Barshefsky, Berman and Commerce Secretary William Daley plan to spend some of their time working the phones and making other contacts to win some undecided lawmakers.
Clinton met with about two dozen House Democrats last week to discuss fast track and planned to meet with more at the White House on Thursday.
"I think we are moving along quite well in terms of laying the groundwork," Barshefsky said.
